stimulus: Hysteresis loops are the obvious place to start, that lazy fat curve where going up and coming down don't retrace each other. But a loop alone doesn't prove memory, because friction or lag could fake it. So people sweep slower and slower, and if the loop survives in the quasi-static limit it's rate-independent, which is the real signature. Then there's the oddity of return-point memory: cycle a magnet inside a minor loop and it remembers the turning points, like a stack of nested bookmarks, and erases them when you exceed a bigger extremum. Wiping rules! Preisach models treat the material as a crowd of tiny bistable switches, each flipping at its own threshold, which makes me think of coin-sorting machines. Kids learn about this with crumpled paper, which keeps its creases. Then Keim and Nagel's work on memory in sheared or cyclically driven suspensions: you train a system at one amplitude and read the amplitude back out later, like a tape recorder made of mud. Reading out is destructive sometimes, which is irritating. Annealing erases it, so does heating past a critical temperature. Shape-memory alloys, meanwhile, remember by crystal phase, not by switches, and that's a different mechanism wearing the same costume. Aging in glasses shows memory too, via the Kovacs effect, where volume relaxes non-monotonically after a temperature jump. Why does that feel like a clue?

Research question: "What analyses or measurements would best test whether AP-1 acts as a cellular memory mechanism?"

Propose 5 distinct, concrete ideas (analyses, measurements, or experiments) that a research lab could pursue to address this question. For each idea give a short title and a description of one or two sentences.

ideas.title: Rate-independent hysteresis of AP-1 target output
ideas.description: Ramp a stimulus (e.g., optogenetic or chemically induced ERK/JNK activation, or serum) up and down at progressively slower rates, and measure c-Fos/c-Jun levels, chromatin accessibility and target-gene transcription in single cells. A loop that persists in the quasi-static limit shows true rate-independent memory rather than kinetic lag from slow protein or mRNA turnover, and a lag-only model can be fitted and rejected.

ideas.title: Return-point memory via nested minor-loop stimulation
ideas.description: Drive cells with nested sequences of stimulus amplitudes (up to A1, down to B1, up to A2<A1, and so on) and read out AP-1 occupancy and reporter activity at each turning point. If the system keeps nested bookmarks of earlier extrema, and a larger excursion erases the smaller ones, that supports a Preisach-like population of AP-1 sites with distinct thresholds, as opposed to one global state variable.

ideas.title: Preisach-style decomposition of AP-1 enhancers from single-cell multiome data
ideas.description: Use ATAC-seq, CUT&Tag for FOS/JUN and RNA-seq after stimulation at graded doses and durations to estimate each enhancer's on and off thresholds, then test whether the whole-population response is reproduced by a distribution of independent bistable switches. Sites that open at a high threshold and close only at a much lower one are the memory elements, and a model built from these thresholds can be used to predict held-out stimulus histories.

ideas.title: Training-and-readout of amplitude memory plus erasure tests
ideas.description: Train cells with repeated pulses at a defined amplitude or frequency, rest them for varying times, and then probe with a test stimulus to see whether the response depends on the training amplitude, as in the Keim–Nagel protocol. Compare readout with a single probe versus repeated probes to test whether reading is destructive. Test erasure by AP-1 dominant-negative (A-FOS) expression, by cell division or by a pulse larger than the trained one. Also test whether the memory depends on pioneer-like remodeling by perturbing SWI/SNF or histone modifiers.

ideas.title: Kovacs-like non-monotonic relaxation after a perturbation
ideas.description: Apply a step change in stimulus or signaling, such as a transient JNK/ERK inhibitor or activator pulse, and track AP-1 activity and chromatin state as they relax. Compare the trajectories of two preparations that reach the same instantaneous AP-1 level through different histories. Different later relaxation, such as non-monotonic overshoot, shows the cell carries hidden state variables beyond the AP-1 level, for example chromatin accessibility or partner-factor composition. Perturbing these hidden variables can then separate a switch-like mechanism from a phase-like one.
